title: Table-driven tests, t.Run, t.Helper, t.Cleanup, t.Context
summary: A Go test is ordinary code: a table of cases, a loop, t.Run for named subtests, and if got != want { t.Errorf(...) }. Helpers call t.Helper and register their own t.Cleanup; t.Context ends with the test.

examples.title: A table of cases, one subtest per row

annotations.note: The table is a slice of an anonymous struct, one row per case, each with a name. Adding a case is one line; the checking code below is written once. An err field compared with errors.Is covers success and failure rows alike, because errors.Is(nil, nil) is true.
"1,234" reads as one thousand to an English eye and is invalid in Turkish notation. Locale traps like this are cheap to pin down once they are a row in a table.
t.Run makes each row a subtest with its own PASS/FAIL line and name. Spaces become underscores and ş is kept, so go test -run 'TestParseKurus/kuruş' runs that row alone.

t.Parallel pauses the subtest until the loop has finished, then runs the paused ones together (the PAUSE and CONT lines). Before Go 1.22 every closure shared one tt: all seven subtests checked the last row and passed. Old code has tt := tt here for that reason.

No assertion library: an if and a message in the form F(input) = got, want want. Fatalf ends this subtest, since comparing values after a wrong error is noise; Errorf records the failure and lets the test continue.

examples.title: Helpers with t.Helper, t.Cleanup, t.TempDir and t.Context

annotations.note: A helper takes t, fails the test itself and returns a ready value. t.Helper makes failures and logs inside it report the caller's line: the output shows "journal opened" at line 52, in TestJournal, while logWithoutHelper's message points at its own line 48.
t.TempDir creates a fresh directory per test and registers a cleanup that deletes it, so nothing leaks between tests or runs.

The helper registers the Close itself, so no caller can forget it. Cleanups run last-in, first-out: this one, registered after TempDir's, closes the file before the directory is removed. On Windows, deleting a directory with an open file fails the test.
t.Context() (Go 1.24) is already canceled when cleanups run, which the log shows. Cleanup code that still needs to talk to something, such as a database rollback, uses context.Background().
The closure in a cleanup is not a helper, so its log line points here. It runs before the helper's cleanup because it was registered later.
Pass t.Context() to the code under test: it is canceled as soon as the test function returns, so goroutines the test started see Done before the cleanups wait for them.

examples.title: Comparing without an assertion library: slices.Equal, DeepEqual, %+q

annotations.note: Table-driven without t.Run is fine for fast, independent rows: the loop reports every failing row with Errorf and keeps going. Use t.Run when you want names, -run filtering or parallelism.
slices.Equal (Go 1.21) compares element by element with == and treats nil and empty as equal. %+q prints strings with non-ASCII escaped, so a failure message shows exactly which code points differ.
strings.Fields returns an empty, non-nil slice. reflect.DeepEqual tells nil and empty apart, so a test written with DeepEqual against nil would fail although the behaviour is right.

JavaScript's toLowerCase applies Unicode's full mapping and turns İ into i plus U+0307 COMBINING DOT ABOVE; Go's ToLowerSpecial with TurkishCase gives a plain i. %q shows two strings that look alike; %+q shows the escaped U+0307 that makes them unequal.

use_cases: Parsers, validators and formatters: one row per input, including the locale and boundary cases that bite
Error paths: a want-error column checked with errors.Is, next to the success rows
Shared setup (temp files, servers, database connections) wrapped in a helper that calls t.Helper and registers its own t.Cleanup
Code that starts goroutines or takes a context: pass t.Context() so it stops when the test does
strengths: No framework to learn: tests are plain Go, so the debugger, refactoring tools and the race detector work on them unchanged, unlike Jest's or pytest's runtime magic
Errorf keeps going after a failure, so one run reports every broken row, where a JUnit assertEquals throws and hides the rest of the method
Subtests give every row a name that -run can select and that CI reports separately, with no @ParameterizedTest or test.each annotation layer
t.Cleanup lets a helper own its teardown, so the setup and its undo sit together instead of in a separate @AfterEach or afterEach
weaknesses: Messages are written by hand; without a library there is no automatic diff of two large structs (teams that want one usually allow github.com/google/go-cmp)
reflect.DeepEqual is strict about nil versus empty and compares unexported fields, so it fails on differences that don't matter
t.Fatal only works from the test's own goroutine; goroutines the test starts must report back over a channel or use t.Error

pitfalls.title: Parallel subtests on a pre-1.22 go line
pitfalls.detail: With go 1.21 or older in go.mod, every closure shares the loop variable: all subtests test the last row and pass. go test doesn't catch it; go vet's loopclosure check does. Raise the go line, or copy the variable.
pitfalls.bad:
for _, tt := range tests { // module says go 1.21
	t.Run(tt.name, func(t *testing.T) {
		t.Parallel()
		check(t, tt) // always the last row

pitfalls.title: Calling t.Fatal from a goroutine
pitfalls.detail: Fatal stops the goroutine that calls it, via runtime.Goexit. From a goroutine the test started, it ends that goroutine, not the test, and a test waiting for that goroutine's result hangs until go test's timeout. go vet reports "call to (*testing.T).Fatal from a non-test goroutine". Send the error back to the test goroutine, or use t.Error, which only records the failure.

pitfalls.title: Using t.Context() in a cleanup
pitfalls.detail: It is canceled before cleanups run, so a rollback or close that takes it fails at once. Use context.Background() there.

pitfalls.title: Leaving files open in t.TempDir
pitfalls.detail: On Windows the directory can't be removed while a file in it is open, and the test fails with "TempDir RemoveAll cleanup" even though Linux CI is green. Close files in a cleanup registered after TempDir.

quiz.q: What is the difference between t.Errorf and t.Fatalf?
options: Both fail the test; Fatalf also stops the current test or subtest
Fatalf exits the whole test binary
quiz.why: Errorf marks the test failed and continues; Fatalf marks it failed and calls runtime.Goexit, ending only that test's goroutine.

quiz.q: A helper calls t.Helper() and then t.Fatalf. Which line does the failure message show?
options: The t.Fatalf line inside the helper
The line in the test that called the helper
quiz.why: Helper marks the function as a helper, and the testing package reports the first caller that isn't one.

quiz.q: In what order do t.Cleanup functions run?
quiz.why: They run last-in, first-out after the test and its subtests finish, so later resources are released before the ones they depend on.

options: Just before the Cleanup functions run
After all Cleanup functions have run
quiz.why: The docs specify cancellation just before cleanups, so cleanups can wait for goroutines that stop on Done.

further_reading.title: Go FAQ: Where is my favorite helper function for testing?
Go Code Review Comments: Useful Test Failures

body:
## Concept

A test is a function `func TestXxx(t *testing.T)` in a file ending in `_test.go`.
`go test` compiles the package together with its test files into a test binary and runs
every `Test` function. There are no assertions: you compare with `==`, `errors.Is` or
`slices.Equal` and report with `t.Errorf` (record a failure, keep going) or `t.Fatalf`
(record it and stop this test).

The idiomatic shape is the **table-driven test**: a slice of cases, each a row with a
name, inputs and the expected result, and one loop that checks them all. `t.Run(name, f)`
turns each row into a **subtest** with its own name, result line and `-run` filter.

The rest of `*testing.T` keeps tests short and clean:

- `t.Helper()` marks a function as a helper, so failures point at the caller.
- `t.Cleanup(f)` registers teardown; cleanups run last-in, first-out when the test ends.
- `t.TempDir()`, `t.Setenv(k, v)` and `t.Chdir(dir)` (Go 1.24) undo themselves.
- `t.Context()` (Go 1.24) is a context canceled just before the cleanups run.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **GoogleTest**: `EXPECT_EQ` keeps going and `ASSERT_EQ` stops the test; that is exactly
  `t.Errorf` versus `t.Fatalf`. `TEST_P` parameterized tests are a table and a loop.
- **JUnit 5**: `@ParameterizedTest` with `@MethodSource` is the table; `assertEquals`
  becomes an `if`. `@AfterEach` becomes a `t.Cleanup` registered by the helper that
  created the resource.
- **pytest**: `@pytest.mark.parametrize` is the table; a fixture with `yield` is a helper
  that returns a value and registers `t.Cleanup`. Go has no assert rewriting, so the
  message you write is the message you get.
- **Jest/Vitest**: `test.each` is the table, `expect(x).toEqual(y)` becomes
  `slices.Equal` or `==` plus `t.Errorf`, and `afterEach` becomes `t.Cleanup`.

## How it works

`go test` runs top-level tests one after another in source order. A subtest that calls
`t.Parallel()` pauses until its parent's function returns, then runs alongside its
paused siblings; the parent finishes only when all of them have. That is why the
`-v` output shows `=== PAUSE` and `=== CONT` lines, and why the summary lines can come
in a different order each run.

When a test fails, the output names the test, the file and the line of the `t.Errorf`
call (or of the caller, for a helper). Real output from changing one row of the first
example to expect `1234560`:

```
--- FAIL: TestParseKurus (0.00s)
    --- FAIL: TestParseKurus/thousands (0.00s)
        01_table_test.go:52: ParseKurus("1.234,56") = 123456, want 1234560
FAIL
FAIL	lesson	1.695s
FAIL
```

`-run` takes one regular expression per subtest level, separated by `/`:
`go test -run 'TestParseKurus/kuruş' -v` runs only the `only_kuruş` row. `-v` prints
`t.Log` output and a line per test; without it, only failures are printed.

## Design notes

The Go FAQ explains the missing assertions: a test should report everything that is
wrong in one run, with a message that someone who doesn't know the code can act on. A
table amortizes the cost of that message over every row. Write it as
`F(input) = got, want want`, quote strings with `%q` (or `%+q` when non-ASCII text can
hide a difference), and compare with the narrowest tool: `==` for comparable values and
structs, `errors.Is` for errors, `slices.Equal` and `maps.Equal` for collections, and
`reflect.DeepEqual` only when nothing else fits.

Put setup in helpers that take `t`, call `t.Helper()`, fail the test themselves and
register their own cleanup. Tests then read as a list of facts instead of setup code,
and teardown can't be forgotten. Give code under test `t.Context()` rather than
`context.Background()`, so anything it starts stops when the test does; in cleanups,
which run after that cancellation, use `context.Background()`.
